notes.title: Windows on walls we had no photo of
notes.text: Large modelled buildings used to draw any wall without a photo as one blank plane. Those walls now show a window grid unless a photo shows the wall really is blind; 60 buildings were checked one by one and updated, and halls, car parks and metal-clad sheds wait for a better fit. The Kromhout yard's west halls on the Gedempt Hamerkanaal are blue-grey metal with their real window row, the Buitenzagerij gallery block on Het Dok shows its galleries (and its card now says Amsterdam-Noord, not the Jordaan), and the Kazerne Hendrik's curved wall has its paired windows.

notes.title: No more glass hats on new-build roofs
notes.text: Many blocks built since 2005 wore a bright blue glass top storey, added at random. Aerial photos show those roofs carry solar panels and plant, not glass, so 852 roofs are back to their real flat tops; only buildings known to have a set-back top floor keep one. On Grasweg in Noord, a glass band that floated over the two modelled towers and roofed their courtyard is gone too. From far away the pre-built city may still show a few until its next rebuild.

notes.title: No more stale destinations after a reload
notes.text: A ride left open overnight no longer brings back yesterday's destination. When you reload, a stored next stop the game would not choose today (such as Meerpadkerk) is swapped for a better-known place, unless you picked it yourself. A ride paused with the tab closed now ends after three hours. Home rides and stand-in destinations also favour well-known places over obscure ones nearby.

notes.title: Bridge railings on the outer edge, paths flat under motorway bridges
notes.text: On the A10 bridges at Ringweg-Noord the railing now stands on the outer edge of the road instead of in the middle of the hard shoulder. Where a bridge deck narrows over the water, its railing follows the edge smoothly instead of stepping in and out. At Lelylaan the cycle paths and streets that pass under the Ringweg-West bridges stay on the ground instead of tearing up to the bridge edge. Across the city, about a quarter fewer metres of railing stand in traffic.

notes.title: De Hallen's windows sit on its wall again
notes.text: De Hallen's windows and gable ends now sit on the stepped brick front on the Bellamyplein side instead of hanging up to 6 m in front of it. A new check measures every window and door in every landmark model against its wall whenever a landmark is rebuilt, so floating windows can't slip in unnoticed.

notes.title: Flats are no longer drawn as grey industrial sheds
notes.text: Some blocks of flats and listed buildings were drawn as blank grey or cream industrial sheds, because the list of building uses we read had dropped every dwelling. Any building with homes in it, a listed monument, a tower, or a small or tall unmapped building now keeps its ordinary look. About 700 buildings changed, 11 of them in the centre. Some of them still get too many window columns; that is a separate fix.

notes.title: Roof ridges run the way the real roofs do
notes.text: Pitched and gabled roofs used to guess their ridge from the building's longest side, which put gable ends facing the street on many rows that really have long roofs along it (Jan Hanzenstraat, Bilderdijkkade). Roofs now turn to the ridge measured by 3DBAG wherever it has one: wrongly turned roofs drop from about 68 % to 16 % of the 27,000 roofs we can check. Bilderdijkkade's 1895 houses have no measured slope at all, so they are unchanged for now.

images.caption: Jan Hanzenstraat from above, same pose: before | after. Look at the back row: the sawtooth of gable ends becomes continuous roofs.

notes.title: Ordinary houses are back on their plots
notes.text: Since early October every ordinary house was drawn a little too far from the city centre: about 1.5 m in the canal belt and up to about 4 m at the edge of the city, on both the map view and the street-level view. Two parts of the game used slightly different sizes for the Earth. Next to the houses that have their own models (which were placed correctly) this showed as houses overlapping their neighbours and gaps between them: the overlaps and gaps on this morning's Haarlemmerdijk picture. The wrong gables and the poor likeness on that picture were faults in the models themselves; five of its six houses are now held or waiting for review. Measured on 19,719 houses in the centre, the worst error drops from 4.4 m to 1.6 m, and 95 % of houses are now within half a metre. A smaller error remains far north and south of the centre: calculated at about 1.3 m at Zuidas and more in Zuidoost, still to be measured and fixed.

notes.title: No more random drainpipes or ladder stripes
notes.text: We removed the drainpipes that were scattered over 40 % of all walls, and the pale ladder-like strips on some modern blocks. Those were decorative fins placed every 1.5 m regardless of the windows; they now appear only where a building record calls for them. Street furniture such as bins now loads around you rather than around the point the camera looks at.

notes.title: Buildings stand on the pavement again on raised streets
notes.text: Buildings along raised streets now stand on the pavement instead of sinking into it. At the Kinkerbrug, Postjesweg's shopfronts and front doors are back above the street, and the lower yard sides show a plinth instead. City-wide, about 37,500 buildings had more than 2 m of front wall buried; 852 remain, mostly in odd pits.

notes.title: Rides head for places worth knowing
notes.text: New riders now start and finish at Amsterdam's well-known landmarks, like the Westerkerk and the Rijksmuseum, instead of a random neighbourhood building; lesser-known places open up as you learn the streets around them. Duplicate destinations are gone (Westertoren and Westerkerk are one stop now) and 17 notable places joined, including the Bijbels Museum.

notes.title: Landmark cards wait for the street the building faces
notes.text: The building card and the "Which building is this?" question now open only when you are on the street the building actually fronts. The Krijtberg no longer pops up from the Herengracht with only its spires showing; it opens from the Singel, in front of its entrance.

notes.title: "Which building is this?" waits until you are beside it
notes.text: The building question used to open as far as 150 m away, sometimes about a building round the corner you could not see. Now it opens only when you are right beside the building (about 35 m from its frontage), including when you turn a corner and find it alongside you. "On the left" or "on the right" now points at the building itself.

notes.title: 175 canal-belt house models: faults found, 24 held
notes.text: Correction to this morning's note. The 175 canal-belt houses modelled from their photos (Burgwallen-Oude Zijde, the Nieuwmarkt, the western canal belt, Haarlemmerdijk) were accepted on counts, not checked in the street, and the picture below shows faults that check should have caught: houses that look shifted into their neighbours, gaps, one gable drawn badly, one house too small, and one missing the raised dormer it has in the photo. A check of every model against its building outline found 24 that fail: walls standing forward of the street line, pushing into a neighbouring house, or with the wrong gable. Those 24 are held, and the ordinary generator draws them again from their measured specs. The overlaps on Haarlemmerdijk turn out to involve a neighbouring house drawn off its plot in the view this picture was taken from; whether players see the same is being checked now, and the five houses in the picture are held or released on that result.

notes.title: Scan Hunt: find art to LiDAR-scan for the ride
notes.text: A small field page at https://rideamsterdam.nl/scan.html lists the public art nearest to you that the ride would like a phone LiDAR scan of: 1,285 pieces that are not in the game yet, and 38 hand-made statue models that a scan would improve. It shows the distance and a direction arrow, and gives points, levels and badges for each piece you mark as scanned (kept on your phone only). It also explains the scanning method: Scaniverse, Mesh mode, export GLB, name the file with the card's code and drop it in the iCloud Drive folder "Ride scans".

notes.title: Rows of houses vary like the real street
notes.text: Unmeasured houses used to take one middle colour from their measured neighbours, so whole rows came out the same grey-brown. Each house now picks its own colour from the middle of what was measured nearby. The change per house is small: on 146 photo comparisons the average wall colour error went from 0.097 to 0.091. It shows most where a pale house sat in a dark row (Herenstraat, first picture); elsewhere it is hard to see. Pale painted fronts are still drawn too dark; they need a photo of each house.

notes.title: Tunnels, underpasses and rail bridges from a checked list
notes.text: Where roads dip under the ring, the A10 and the railways, the ground used to be shaped by guesswork from map data, which sometimes left a ramp in the wrong place or a deck over a tram that runs at street level. A hand-checked list of crossings, each compared with the aerial photo and a street panorama, now decides where the road goes under, where a deck spans it and where the tunnel mouth opens. It covers the IJtunnel, Piet Heintunnel, the ring roads and the railway underpasses.

notes.title: House walls take their colour from measured neighbours
notes.text: Houses we haven't measured from a photo used to draw a guessed colour: white, slate grey or orange terracotta, which had nothing to do with the real street. They now borrow the measured wall colour of nearby houses from the same period, and measured walls keep their real, muted colour instead of being pushed toward orange-red. The city reads darker and browner, closer to the photos: on 114 photo comparisons the wall colour error fell by a third. Rows can look too uniform where nothing nearby has been measured; more variety is being tested next.

notes.title: Fewer made-up gables
notes.text: Listed houses used to get the gable named in the monuments register even where today's front has none. Now a register gable is drawn only where the 3D roof data shows a crown above the eaves, and a gable read from a street photo always wins. Of the roughly 2,500 register gables the game draws itself, about 125 change: about half become the flat fronts they really have, the rest take the mansard, pitched or hipped roof the data shows. The other 2,350 keep their gable, and the 90 on individually modelled buildings are untouched. The old gable is kept as a fact for the house's card.

notes.title: The ground around you finishes sooner
notes.text: At the start of a ride the ground right around you now finishes building half a second to a second and a half sooner on the same start. The ground builders used to let a tile outside your block jump the queue when it sat next to one they already held; a free builder now only picks among tiles of the same level and the same side of your block.

notes.title: The IJ-tunnel's west ramp keeps its wall
notes.text: The IJ-tunnel's west ramp now keeps its wall all the way down: no more street draped into the trench halfway along. The east bank rises nine metres in one run, which the wall scan had read as too wide to be a wall, so the wall stopped for 48 metres and the verge above folded into the cutting.

notes.title: The ground is there when the ride starts
notes.text: The ground under the camera now begins building during the loading screen and is in place about a second sooner after the reveal, and the ride is revealed no later than before. The ground builders no longer queue up behind each other: each takes the next most urgent cell as soon as it is free, prefers cells next to ones it already holds, and a finished cell is never built twice.

notes.title: Clean tunnel mouths under the Prins Hendrikkade
notes.text: The IJ-tunnel's mouths under the Prins Hendrikkade junction are clean: no more pale paving sheets hanging into the mouths, and the street over the tunnel no longer sags beside the ramps' cycle path. The height model had dropped the covered junction by two metres, so the mouth tops sat in a dip and the ground beyond them draped into the trenches; the mouths now rise to the street and the ground is cut at their faces.

notes.title: A smoother start
notes.text: When the loading screen lifts, the view no longer slides down into place over the first quarter second, and the big landmarks next to where your ride begins (the Rijksmuseum at Museumplein, Centraal Station) are already in place instead of popping in a moment later. The first frame you see is the frame the ride starts from. Measured on a Mac the largest change in any frame after the reveal fell from 7-13 % of the picture to under 1 %, at a cost of about a tenth of a second before the ride starts.

notes.title: Bridges keep their road
notes.text: The carriageway and the red cycle path now run unbroken across the Kattenburgerbrug and the Prins Hendrikkade bridges instead of breaking into a pale band at each end, and a junction mouth draws one red crossing, not two. At the Beltbrug a grass verge no longer greys the cycle path. The cause was the ground-level footways under each bridge end, drawn at kerb height above the deck.

notes.title: Tunnel ramps and junctions tidied
notes.text: The IJ-tunnel ramps no longer have pale paving and grass sheets hanging over their walls: ground that crossed a tunnel wall is now cut at the wall, each side at its own level. Across the city the tiny stray paving specks and kerb stubs at junctions are gone (12,000 slivers merged into their neighbours, 2,300 kerb stubs under 1.5 m removed), visibly at Muntplein and by Arcam on the Prins Hendrikkade. Some pale sheets remain along the ramp sides that have no wall; that is the next fix.

notes.title: Flat roofs read as roofs, not bright slabs
notes.text: Flat roofs seen from the air are no longer one bright slab. Their tone now matches the aerial photograph (14 of the 15 largest lids around the Nieuwmarkt sit within a shade of it, against 4 before), the surface carries the grain and seams of gravel and membrane, large roofs show a roof box, and a parapet lip appears as you come closer. The city's simplified shells were re-baked with the same roofs.

notes.title: Tapping a named place says what it is
notes.text: Tapping a named place now tells you what it is (a Sikh gurdwara, a Roman Catholic church, a gift shop), even when the building record itself is blank. The Shri Guru Nanak Gurdwara Sahib used to say it had no name or date; its card now reads "A Sikh gurdwara at Schakelstraat 21" with a link to its map source. About 900 places got a clearer description (62 Protestant and 61 Roman Catholic churches, 45 mosques, shop kinds such as "a gift shop" instead of "a gift"), and 722 public artworks became tappable.

notes.title: Flying over the city is easier on your computer
notes.text: Panning the city from the air no longer runs the fan flat out. While the camera flies it draws at 30 frames a second and redraws the sun's shadows only every few frames; the moment you stop, the view is drawn at full rate and full sharpness again. Measured on an M4 Pro Mac the graphics card went from fully busy to about a third while panning, with the still picture unchanged.

Around Sloterdijk the A10, A5 and S101 badges repeated every few hundred metres along the same road; each road now carries one badge per visible stretch. notes.text: Roofs sit back on their walls along the Stadhouderskade, the Singelgracht and the Geldersekade. notes.title: The Weesperstraat slab no longer shimmers
notes.text: The tall 1962 slab on Weesperstraat no longer shimmers while you ride past it. On desktop, where a facade's window grid shrinks to a few pixels, the renderer now blends nine samples across each pixel instead of one, which takes the moiré out of the long wall; a little fine detail at that distance is traded for calm. Phones keep the previous behaviour for now.

notes.title: Flying over the city is smooth
notes.text: Two more fixes for the flight over Amsterdam on desktop. The map now loads only the ground within about a kilometre and a half of where you are looking, instead of the whole view at once (the far horizon is drawn by the simpler far tier, as before), so a new district no longer arrives as one big parcel. And the trees update about four times faster from the air: each map tile's trees are prepared once and only reassembled when something changes. On a three-minute flight across the city there are now no frames over a tenth of a second (there were 9 to 10 after the last fix, 38 to 52 before it). Nothing looks different up close. Add ?ringFootprint=0 or ?treesIncremental=0 to the ride link to compare. Phones are unchanged until measured.

notes.title: Flying over the city hitches less
notes.text: Panning across Amsterdam from the air used to stutter each time a new district came into view: the whole district arrived in one go, and the ride spent a second or two handing every building, tree and baked block over at once. The arrivals are now spread out, nearest the middle of the view first, so a desktop flight across the city stays smooth (frames over a tenth of a second on a three-minute flight: 8 to 12, from 38 to 52). Nothing is missing; a far district simply fades in over a moment instead of all at once. Add ?arrivalPace=0 to the ride link to compare. Phones are unchanged until measured.

notes.title: The baked city from the air is back on
notes.text: Earlier this evening the baked city from the air was switched off for a few hours after a test showed the canal houses missing at some chase heights. That turned out to be the test holding the camera still, not the ride: with the game running, the houses were always there. It is on again on desktop, and the fade that brings each baked block in no longer depends on the camera moving. Add ?bakedCoarse=0 to the ride link to compare.

notes.title: Above-ground waste boxes, and a better litter bin
notes.text: Where there is no room underground, mostly in the 19th-century ring, Amsterdam uses big above-ground boxes for rest, paper, glass and textile. The ride now draws all 895 of them from the city's register: a graphite box on a steel frame with a high throw-in hatch, standing where the register puts it, like the pair on Nassaukade at the Da Costakade. The litter bin in the gallery is rebuilt too: its opening is now cut into the hood instead of floating in front of it.

The coarse city is baked ahead of time per cell and streamed in as one piece, so a pan over one area keeps its buildings still; the few fades left happen when you jump to a new district. notes.text: Panning across the city from the air is smoother: the building bases that used to be re-fitted to the ground on every aerial frame now wait until you come back down, and are then fitted in small slices. notes.text: From the air, the map shows just a handful of landmark names plus neighbourhood and water names, and labels no longer jump around while you pan. notes.title: The turn-pad hint sits centred in its bar
notes.text: On phones, the one-line hint above the turn pad ("tap to ride — ◀ ▶ turn at the next corner, ↺ turns round") is now vertically centred in its rounded bar instead of sitting a little low.

notes.title: Waste containers stand in a row, on their plates
notes.text: Underground waste containers now line up along the kerb the way they do on the street, evenly spaced and all facing the same way. Each one stands on its steel base plate, which used to vanish under the pavement.

notes.title: Underground containers at their true width
notes.text: The underground waste containers on the street corners are now as wide as the real ones. Each has angled corner strips, access doors on the sides and the three Amsterdam crosses. A dark front panel carries a light bag, bottle or sheet. Glass has its round hole in the slope and paper its slot, each under a yellow or blue band across the top. The rest container's stainless drum sits in the slope above the lip.

notes.title: Sharper windows on big screens
notes.text: On desktop, window frames, glass and glazing bars are now drawn crisply, and the brick and trim around them are sharper too. Window grids no longer shimmer when you pan. Phones keep the previous look for now (try ?windowSdf=1 on a phone to preview it).

notes.title: The Atrium on the Zuidas
notes.text: Riding along Strawinskylaan or Parnassusweg, you now pass the Atrium as it stands. The 1974 NMB headquarters has its light aluminium grid and granite shafts, with the T-shaped window high on the Parnassusweg shaft. The round-cornered Zuidtoren and north-east block are banded with bronze floor slabs that pull back from the corners, and the ATRIUM letters stand on the canopy over the entrance.

notes.title: The Symphony towers at Gustav Mahlerplein
notes.text: At Gustav Mahlerplein, both Symphony towers now show their deep orange-red brick fins, with the windows set back between them and a row of merlons along the crown, where before they were flat striped boxes.

notes.title: Xavier on the Gustav Mahlerlaan
notes.text: The stepped brick tower of Xavier now rises in its three tiers over the Mahlerlaan, with dark slab edges and balcony stacks, and the XAVIER letters over the courtyard gate.

notes.title: The Sint-Nicolaaslyceum on the Beethovenplein
notes.text: The Sint-Nicolaaslyceum now shows its rounded concrete storey bands and the 12 m cantilever over the schoolyard, with its name in red on the deck wall.

notes.title: Het Boekhuis on the Kingsfordweg
notes.text: The Kingsfordweg book distribution centre, now home to the Belastingdienst, stands as its own model: a glass-gridded office slab with wide low window bands over the long warehouse halls.

notes.title: Vliegbasis De Huygens on the Jan Evertsenstraat
notes.text: The 1968 Dominicus Savius technical school on the Jan Evertsenstraat, now Vliegbasis De Huygens, has its hooked block with ribbon window bands, the arched glass workshops, the west glass end and the yellow entrance pavilion.

notes.title: EDGE Stadium by the Olympic Stadium
notes.text: Atelier PRO's former Forum offices by the Olympic Stadium, now EDGE Stadium: two shifted wings of windows over dark spandrels with sandstone ends, and the light glass serre added in 2022.

notes.title: Valerius on the Valeriusplein
notes.text: The new dark-brick Valerius block on the Valeriusplein, on the site of the former Valeriuskliniek, with its light-grey window surrounds, pergolas, terraces stepping into the garden and the garden fence.

notes.title: Het Amsterdams Lyceum on the Valeriusplein
notes.text: The Baanders brothers' 1920 school on the Valeriusplein is now modelled. You can ride through its carriage arches under the reliefs "Potius deficere quam desperare" and "In het eerste vredesjaar", past the four towers, the white-framed windows and the 1920 clock.

notes.title: Doorways now stand back from the wall
notes.text: On President Steynstraat, Zaanhof, Polanenstraat, Albert Luthulistraat, Hasebroekstraat and Eerste Helmersstraat, front doors now sit in brick reveals and portieken at depths measured from street panoramas, instead of flat on the wall. Zaanhof's and Polanenstraat's arched entrances are real arched openings. The jambs inside each reveal darken toward the door, as in the photos; this also shows on Eerste and Derde Helmersstraat, Schalk Burgerstraat and Cornelis Anthoniszstraat. Each strip shows the panorama, the old flat door, the new reveal, and the rider's view before and after.

notes.title: The Oude Turfmarkt river front
notes.text: The whole Oude Turfmarkt river front between the Rokin and the Grimburgwal is now modelled: the stone Nederlandsche Bank front with its pediment, the University's neo-Renaissance front, the banded St. Bernardus and the canal houses between them, each with its own windows, gables and white bands.

notes.title: Het Noortse Bosch on the Vijzelgracht
notes.text: Het Noortse Bosch on the Vijzelgracht, the AFM's stepped dark-brick office block, now stands with its six storeys of narrow white windows, its glazed hall along the Lijnbaansgracht, the copper caps on its stepped tops and the copper stair strip.

notes.title: The Barlaeus Gymnasium on the Weteringschans
notes.text: The Barlaeus Gymnasium on the Weteringschans is now modelled: its sandstone street front with the GYMNASIUM attic and its sculpture group, the pedimented end pavilions and the arched portico, and the banded brick side along the Lijnbaansgracht.

notes.title: The former C&A block on the Damrak
notes.text: The former C&A block on the Damrak is now modelled with its 2016 brick-and-stone front: five double-height shopfronts under paired white stone oriels, white bands across the red brick, the Beurspassage arch and the corner tower, and the banded bays on the Nieuwendijk side.

notes.title: The DoubleTree hotel by Centraal Station
notes.text: The DoubleTree hotel by Centraal Station is now modelled on the Oosterdok: its stepped dark-brick block with grey-banded hotel windows up to the top storeys, the two-storey glazed restaurant floor between brick piers under the terrace pergola, and the white panelled entrance drum.

notes.title: Kinkerstraat 89-105 on the corner of the Tollensstraat
notes.text: The 1987 corner block on the Kinkerstraat, Tollensstraat and Bilderdijkkade is now drawn individually. Its window bands, loggia bays and corner match the city panoramas.

notes.title: The Postjesweg police station
notes.text: The 2004 red-brick police station at Postjesweg 179 now stands in the game. It has its ribbon window, louvred upper windows, the POLITIE sign, the garage doors and the corner pergola balcony.

notes.title: Quarter Plaza on the Transformatorweg
notes.text: Riders on the Transformatorweg now pass Quarter Plaza: a brick slab with long ribbon windows lifted on raked V-columns over a glass lobby, its "quarter plaza" and "tot maandag" lettering, and the long white office bar on pilotis beside it.

notes.title: Winkelcentrum Plein '40-'45 in Slotermeer
notes.text: The shopping centre beside the square is now drawn as it stands. It has the seven-storey block with staggered blue balconies over the mall entrance, the brick garage with its rhythm of louvred slots and orange columns, the housing bar over a shop canopy, and the grey office bar under its raked pergola.

notes.title: The Andreas Ensemble on the Cornelis Lelylaan
notes.text: The 2009 block with the WestCord Fashion Hotel is now drawn individually. On the Lelylaan, the stepped buff-brick front rises over a two-storey stone plinth of shops and glass-block bays. The 41 m hotel tower carries its lettering, its stone bands and its bay windows. The Titus van Rijnstraat wing has its glazed hotel storey and top loggias, and two grey-brick pavilions with corner balconies stand on the south street.

notes.title: Street blocks from the air draw as one piece
notes.text: Street blocks seen from the air now draw as one piece per material, and far-off blocks swap to a light stand-in: about 600 fewer draw calls over the Jordaan and around the Rijksmuseum. At street level the blocks look the same. Add ?chunkMerge=0 or ?chunkLod2=0 to the ride link to compare.

notes.title: Thin trim stops crawling in the distance
notes.text: Cornices, parapets, railings, signs and other thin façade details no longer shimmer and crawl as you ride: anything thinner than about two screen pixels now fades out smoothly instead of flickering between drawn and not drawn, and trim no longer fights its own wall. Measured on the Weesperstraat slab from your screenshot and at the Hoftuin, Westerkerk and Nassaukade, the moving-pixel count drops 13 to 21 % on whole frames at no visible frame cost. The slab's own window grid still shimmers at a grazing angle; that is the façade texture, not the trim, and the next round owns it. ?thinFade=0 shows the old frame; ?smaa=1 tries a full-screen anti-aliasing pass that is off because it costs 2 to 4 ms. Strips: your shot, before, after, and a 4x crop of the slab.

notes.title: Railways keep their tracks when you look away
notes.text: Pan the map off your bike to the Zuidas or any rail yard and the ground there now builds its ballast beds, sleepers and rails, instead of a flat grey band: the detailed ground used to stay centred on the rider even while you were looking two kilometres away. From high up and on the city map, railways now draw as a dark line on a ballast edge that stays visible on phones, and the distant rails are laid on the land instead of sinking under it. Each strip: aerial photo, your screenshot, before, after.

notes.title: The city runs to the horizon from the air
notes.text: Fly up over Amsterdam and the city no longer stops a kilometre or two from you. Every neighbourhood beyond the streets around the rider is drawn as simple baked blocks out to seven kilometres, so from the Hoftuin, the Zuidas or Bos en Lommer the roofs continue to the skyline instead of ending at an empty beige plain. Map labels also skip their building checks when you fly high, so panning over the whole city is smoother. On the street nothing changes; ?farShells=0 turns the far city off.

notes.title: Sharper distance, steadier rails, and a performance readout
notes.text: Distant buildings now wear their roofs: two to five blocks out, rooftops show their real pitch and colour instead of flat grey lids. When nearby detail fades in, it takes over the simple shape pixel by pixel instead of flickering on top of it. Railway tracks on the ground are drawn as sharp dark rails that stay at least a pixel wide in the distance, instead of blurring into a grey hatch. A new Show performance switch under Comfort & detail puts one small line of numbers in the corner: memory, graphics memory, what is loaded and how smooth the last few seconds were. If the city ever slows down, those numbers tell us why. Flying over the city also keeps far fewer landmark models loaded at once (up to 627 before, about 250 now on a Mac), so a long tour from the air holds about a third less graphics memory.

notes.title: The Bloemenmarkt's sixteen floating stalls, Park Kiosk BEA and Ramon's Coffee
notes.text: The Bloemenmarkt is back on the Singel: all sixteen floating flower stalls from the Koningsplein to the Muntplein end, with their saw-tooth glass roofs, open flower fronts and the canal-side glasshouse wall, placed from the city's mooring register in place of generic houseboats. Park Kiosk BEA in the Beatrixpark stands beside the wading pool as itself, a long low board pavilion with a sedum roof, its kiosk porch and wooden BEA sign at the east end. Ramon's Coffee Kiosk on the Silodam is a small glazed cabin with its dark lettered road side, menu board and a garden on the roof. Pat's Poffertjes turned out to be a shop inside a building, not a kiosk, so it stays in the ordinary building layer.

notes.title: The whole Stedelijk, and the Albert Heijn under the Museumplein
notes.text: The Stedelijk Museum is complete at last: Weissman's red-and-white 1895 building, with its statues, pavilions and clock tower, now joins Benthem Crouwel's white bathtub, and the dark service tower with its ring of STEDELIJK MUSEUM AMSTERDAM lettering stands at the corner instead of a stray house. Across the plaza the Museumplein's grass corner rises over the Albert Heijn's glass front, edged in green copper, with the garage stair kiosks beside it. Measured from the city panoramas; the old model was an unmeasured stand-in with the 1895 building as a plain brick box.

notes.title: The AkzoNobel Center's red block, the Ziggo Dome roof and the Volkshotel letters
notes.text: Three small fixes. The AkzoNobel Center no longer sits inside a 41 m red block: its underground car park had been drawn above ground because the height survey gave the garage outline the towers' roofs, and the 52 other garages the BAG registers wholly below street level have gone the same way. The Ziggo Dome's roof is the white membrane the aerial photo shows, not tan gravel. The VOLKSHOTEL roof letters are solid letters standing on their rail instead of a paper-thin sign that floated off it from behind.

notes.title: The underground waste containers, re-modelled from the panoramas
notes.text: The 13,000 underground container tops on the city's corners are rebuilt from the city panoramas: the graphite Amsterdam column with its hooded top, the stainless drum set into the slope, the fraction colour as a band and on the lift handle, and a round glass hole or a paper slot where the waste register says glass or paper. The old model's sides were missing in the ride, so the columns read see-through; they are solid now. Measured on five panoramas (body 1.19 m, front 0.63 m, plate 1.56 m); the wider 2020s box on the Prinsengracht is not yet told apart by the register, so it still gets the column.

notes.title: A smoother first start (engine preview)
notes.text: The very first start of a ride under the engine preview (?engine=own) stutters less: ground work is spread over more frames, houseboat berths are found far faster, trees and street furniture are rebuilt once instead of several times, and the lookup grids the camera and labels need are built while the start screen is still up. On an iPhone the frames over a tenth of a second at a cold start halved; on a desktop none is over a fifth of a second any more. One long garbage-collection pause per start remains and is the next target.

notes.title: Spoiler screening fixed for bridges and canals (engine preview)
notes.text: Under the engine preview, starting a new route replaced the list of names to hide with only that route’s streets, so a bridge, canal or stop name could appear on a point of interest before you answered. Names from every source are now kept together, as in the standard map.

notes.title: Smoother ride starts (engine preview)
notes.text: Starting a ride, changing route or taking the next one under the engine preview (?engine=own) stalls far less: street labels are screened for spoilers only as they come into view instead of all six thousand at once, buildings are grouped once instead of on every update, and ground data is parsed in small slices. On an iPhone there are no more frames over a fifth of a second at a ride start; on a desktop route changes start without a visible hitch. A cold first start still has one long frame, which is the next thing being worked on.

notes.title: A gentler distance haze, and a switch for it
notes.text: The haze over the far city is softer and starts further away: colour drops by half instead of seventy percent, and window detail stays until about 250 m. If you would rather see the whole city sharp, a new Distance haze switch under Comfort & detail turns it off mid-ride.

notes.title: New engine preview: houses stay put when you bump into them
notes.text: In the new engine (?engine=own), riding into a house front made the house vanish, because the rule that lets you see through the Centraal passage fired on any building you touched. It now fires only when your route runs through the building, and it dims instead of hiding.

notes.title: Buildings stop appearing right in front of you
notes.text: The city used to load the next stretch of buildings only when you crossed into a new map tile, which could be sixty metres ahead of you. It now loads as you move, buildings that do change dissolve in and out instead of popping, and the detailed buildings along your route are fetched before you reach them.

notes.title: New engine preview: the sky stops flickering
notes.text: If you ride with the new engine (?engine=own), the sky no longer flashes to cream while the city streams in around you. The flash came from the shader precompiler resetting the canvas clear colour between frames.

notes.title: Tetterode, the old type foundry on the Bilderdijkstraat and Da Costakade
notes.text: The whole Tetterode block in Oud-West was a four-wall recipe box; it is now its six parts, measured from the city panoramas and Marcel Mulder's photographs: the corner house with its iron balconies and slate mansard, the 1898 melkfabriek Holland with its three hardstone arches, ochre bands and lettered frieze, Hartkamp's 1902 factory with the high segmental workshop windows between anchored piers, the 1909 range with twelve axes of cross windows, the LETTERGIETERIJ 'AMSTERDAM' V/H N.TETTERODE frieze and four dormers, the 1940s Merkelbach and Karsten block with its ribbon storeys, tiled bay and frosted half-round on the roof, and the housing at 136-140 with its loggias and portico. The kit learned segmental arch heads.

notes.title: The big Westerdok block behind Centraal
notes.text: The 2008 courtyard block on the Westerdokseiland (Westerdok 608 to 780, Westerdoksdijk, Coffijboomstraat, Leliendaalstraat) was a stepped recipe box; it is now modelled from its 71 roof pieces and the city panoramas: the 7 m passage and the two porches on the west, the deep-set window grid on 3.4 m axes, the white French windows and grey railing panels on the north blocks, the gallery deck with its columns, the three recessed towers in grey brick, timber and slate standing over open courtyard portals, the framed-bay wedge and the punched wedges on the east, stacked balconies with copper balustrades, and the ochre roof pavilions. Rides along the Westerdokskade and the Westerdoksdijk see it on three sides.

notes.title: The Oudemanhuispoort wings on the Kloveniersburgwal, and Kinkerstraat 32-54
notes.text: Two more recipe boxes replaced by measured models. On the Kloveniersburgwal the north and west wings of the old Oude Mannen- en Vrouwengasthuis (the university's Oudemanhuispoort block) now show Marnette's 1927 'schaats' with its skate band, glass-block oriel and chimney, the beige post-war front, the brick front with its dormers, three neck-gabled canal houses with the rijksmonument at number 72 first, the lecture-hall rear on Rusland and the dark Achterburgwal front with its stone tablet. At the De Hallen end of the Kinkerstraat the 1999 block at 32-54 has its red-brown brick grid over the Vomar shop glazing, the beige corner blocks, the loggia stack on the Da Costakade and the mansard dormers of the set-back top floor. The kit learned mansard dormers, rounded bands and capping 3DBAG roofs under a measured front.

notes.title: The Rietveld Academie's dimpled tower, the Fedlev wing and the bridge between them
notes.text: Next to Rietveld's glass box, the 2006 Benthem Crouwel tower was a plain grey slab; it now has its pressed-metal skin of dimples and dark slices, the three first-floor ribbons wrapping the corners, the high ribbons, the glazed studio storeys on the court side and the stepped roof. The 2018 Fedlev wing beside it has its glazed ground storey under the overhang, the expanded-metal screen storey with its loggias and folding shutters, the stair landing on its V-pylon and the GERRIT RIETVELD ACADEMIE / SANDBERG INSTITUUT lettering, and the sloping mesh footbridge joins the two. The kit learned banded curtain walls and pressed-metal grids.

notes.title: Politiebureau Oost on the Linnaeusstraat
notes.text: The 2003 police station at Linnaeusstraat 111 is now its purple-brown brick block with the glazed corner bays, the split-level window grid of the three zones along the street, the recessed entrance bays with the blue POLITIE shield and lettering, the garage door on the south face and the flagpole. All five faces were measured from the city panoramas; it replaces a recipe box that drew 11 columns where the photo has 18.

notes.title: Two police stations in the centre, on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal and the Lijnbaansgracht
notes.text: The 1996 police station at the Nieuwezijds Kolk corner is now its slit-windowed taupe brick block, bronze glass box, copper-glass prow with the POLITIE lettering and flame on both faces over the canopy lobby, concrete piers, lozenge and flagpole. Lijnbaansgracht 219, the 1977 Public Works station by Anna Clasina van Hattem with its cells in the basement, has its 45 m dark-brown front on a 2.41 m window grid, the white first-storey band, the corner canopy, the notch with its terrace, the set-back top storey and the three vehicle openings. Both replace plain recipe boxes that the likeness check failed, and were measured from the city panoramas.

notes.title: The Hofkerk in Watergraafsmeer and the water tower on the Amstelveenseweg
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks. Kropholler's Hofkerk (the H.H. Martelaren van Gorcum on the Linnaeushof, 1929) has its square tower with the pyramid roof, the crossing tower, the west front with its three doors, rose window and clock, the buttressed aisles and the pastorie, built with a new kit wall that cuts round-headed, pointed and flat openings with real reveals. Piet Elling's 1965 water tower on the Amstelveenseweg is its ribbed aluminium cone on six free columns round the twelve-sided shaft, with the glazed control cabin on top; it is open underneath on every side like the real one. Both measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: The Heinekenplein block, the 1995 one next to the brewery
notes.text: The housing-and-shops block that replaced the brewery yard in 1995 was a plain recipe box; it is now modelled from the city panoramas. The nine-storey office tower stands on the Stadhouderskade corner with its 2 x 2 white-framed windows and the corner tower, the long bar runs down the Eerste Van der Helststraat with its two rows of square windows and ribbon windows over the Dirk shopfronts, the red Dirk drum, the Heineken fascia with the red star, the gateway into the court, the car-park entrance and the beige grid front on the square. Every photographed face has its measured window order; the Heineken script is a pixel-font stand-in for now.

notes.title: Rietveld's own academy building, rebuilt from the photos
notes.text: The Gerrit Rietveld Academie on the Fred. Roeskestraat is Rietveld's 1967 glass box, and the game drew it as one long ribbon. It is now its real self: 36 by 10 modules of 2.09 m on the curtain wall, four clear vision bands alternating with frosted bands over the recessed plinth, the white glazed-brick wall with the GERRIT RIETVELD ACADEMIE lettering, the canopy held off the facade, the steel fire stair, the lift tower and the fan deck, and the workshop wing under its saw-tooth sheds. The kit learned north-light shed roofs.

notes.title: The Film Academy on the Markenplein and the Lekstraat tram depot
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks. The Nederlandse Filmacademie on the Markenplein is Koen van Velsen's 1999 building: the concrete frame with its green channel-glass bands and ribbon windows, the open roof terrace at the east corner, the glass-roofed courtyard and the lettering with the round logo. In the Rivierenbuurt the Remise Lekstraat is the 1927 tram depot that still houses GVB trams: the eight saw-tooth lanterns with their glazed north slopes, the sixteen white steel hall windows and clerestory on the Kromme-Mijdrechtstraat, the risalits and the 1927 plaque over the tower door, the curved nine-bay tram front with its folding doors and the yard walls. Measured from the city panoramas and the 2025 orthophoto. The kit learned eight more lower-case letters.

notes.title: The Effectenbeurs, Het Sieraad and the KPN building at Teleport
notes.text: Three more bespoke landmarks. The Effectenbeurs on the Beursplein is Jos Cuypers' 1913 stock exchange: the frontispiece with its pediment and relief group, the two wings and their pavilions, the corner turrets and the clock. Het Sieraad on the Postjesweg is Westerman's 1923 Amsterdam School trade school: the concave entrance front with its Krop sculpture piers and HET SIERAAD lettering, the curved front on the Kostverlorenvaart with its oriels and mansard dormers, the stair towers and the corner figures. Out at Sloterdijk the KPN building on the Teleportboulevard is the 2014 office with its lavender spandrels, its loggias pulled back behind round columns, the open corner voids behind louvres and the signs on the roof. The kit learned pediment figures, multi-pane window grids, stacked floor trays and a few more letters.

notes.title: The concrete silo beside the Graansilo
notes.text: The 1952 concrete grain silo on the Silodam, inhabited since 1999, now stands next to its stone neighbour: the pale slab with its nine storeys of French-balcony windows in eleven columns over the glazed ground storey, the set-back glazed roof storey under its zinc roof, the round steel fire stair spiralling down the south end, the head tower with its gridded windows and portholes, the perforated eave canopies and the white core with its flues. Measured from the city panoramas and Alf van Beem's photographs.

notes.title: The Graansilo on the Silodam
notes.text: The stone grain silo of 1898 by Klinkhamer and Van Gendt on the Silodam, a rijksmonument converted to homes and studios in 2001: two long brick wings of ten bays each with their recessed panels of stacked lights, the corbel-arcade friezes and rosette anchors, the segmental-arched plinth openings, the attic windows in white reveals, the stone cornice and zinc dormers, the set-back glazed roof storey, and the centre tower with its crenellated parapet, corner turrets, slate tent roof and lantern. Measured from the city panoramas and Alf van Beem's photographs. The kit learned corbel arcades and crenellations as reusable outlines.

notes.title: Sarphati Plaza and the Apollo Hotel
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks. Sarphati Plaza on the Rhijnspoorplein is the 1992 corner tower with its glazed drum and the SARPHATI PLAZA lettering curving round it, the brick front with its shop fronts along the Sarphatistraat and the office storeys above. The Apollo Hotel on the point where the Noorder Amstelkanaal meets the Boerenwetering is Albert Boeken's 1934 curved pavilion on the water, with Bodon's 1962 hotel slab and its later wings behind it and the A on the stair tower. The kit learned to set lettering round a curved band and to cut window openings into shared faces.

notes.title: The Edge and the AkzoNobel Center on the Zuidas
notes.text: Two glass office landmarks on the Zuidas. The Edge on the Gustav Mahlerlaan is PLP's 2013 Deloitte building: three wings round the glass atrium that leans toward the A10, tilted solar panels on the south fronts, white piers on the east, the cantilevered glass bay and the Deloitte and AKD signs. The AkzoNobel Center on the Christian Neefestraat is Group A's 2017 head office: the taller wedge with its rounded nose and AkzoNobel lettering, the lower volume wrapping round it, the leaning blue glass plane over the entrance and the two-storey plinth with its timber fins and EARTH lettering. The kit learned lower-case letters for the signs.

notes.title: Pakhuis Australië, De Makroon, the Tolhuis pavilion and the NDSM slipway
notes.text: Four more bespoke landmarks. Pakhuis Australië on the Oostelijke Handelskade is the 1895 warehouse as rebuilt after the 2002 fire, with the Boston housing block riding on top of it. De Makroon closes the corner of the Nieuwe Passeerdersstraat and the Singelgracht in red and yellow brick with its slate entrance tower and the lettered canopy. Across the IJ, the Tolhuis pavilion on the IJpromenade is Arthur Staal's 1970s Shell canteen under its roof of 22 little pyramids, with the hexagonal windows along the canal. At the NDSM wharf the Y-Helling is the eastern slipway: the sloping deck with its seven rows of keel blocks, the red railings and stair, the head block with its red doors, and the Faralda crane beside it. Measured from the city panoramas, the 2025 orthophoto and open photographs.

notes.title: Autopon on the Overtoom and De Joodsche Invalide on the Weesperplein
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks, both rijksmonumenten. Autopon at the end of the Overtoom is Ben Ingwersen's 1961 garage with the gallery flats above it: the curved front with its 42 loggia bays and red-framed windows, the tapered pilotis over the two-tier showroom glass, the red stair tower on the Zocherstraat side and the sawtooth garage hall behind. De Joodsche Invalide on the Weesperplein is J.F. Staal's 1937 Glazen Paleis: the glass corner box on slender columns, the rounded board room under its shell roof, the grey tiled canal wing, the hooded window axes and round stair windows, the curved entrance canopy and Stauthamer's 1950 plaque. Measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: Byzantium and Van Eyck's Burgerweeshuis
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks. Byzantium at the Vondelpark end of the Stadhouderskade is Rem Koolhaas' 1991 block: the dark glass tower, the cream slab with its punched windows and set-back top, the gold drum on its stalk and the public walk under the park-end canopy. Out at the IJsbaanpad the Burgerweeshuis is Aldo van Eyck's 1960 orphanage: one 3.36 m brick-and-concrete module repeated over 300 times under its little domes, the eight big domes over the halls, the staff block and the chimney, all set from the orthophoto and the city panoramas.

notes.title: WTC Amsterdam, the Volkshotel and the Oranje-Nassau Kazerne
notes.text: Three more bespoke landmarks. The WTC on the Zuidas is its stepped blue-glass tiers with the white wing-blade canopy on its Y-columns along the Strawinskylaan and Tower Ten's fins; the curtain-wall grid is drawn at the real 1.8 m pitch. The Volkshotel on the Wibautstraat is the 1965 Volkskrant building again, the concrete-and-glass slab with its roof-terrace structures and lettering. On the Sarphatistraat the Oranje-Nassau Kazerne runs its full 280 m: every window and dormer at its measured axis, the central pediment with the painted arms, the 1990 passage with the ORANJE-NASSAU frieze, the pavilions with their trophy reliefs and the ship relief at the end. Measured from the city panoramas and open photographs; the DeLaMar was already in the game.

notes.title: Rail viaducts no longer sit as blocks on the tracks
notes.text: Around the stations, the railway viaducts and decks that were drawn as solid buildings over the tracks are gone, and platform canopies are cut to their real shape, as they already were on the older map.

notes.title: Ziggo Dome and the VU hoofdgebouw
notes.text: Two big Zuid landmarks from the round-4 lanes. The Ziggo Dome beside the ArenA is its black box with the LED-rod skin, the window rows behind it, the loading docks on the south-west side, the roof plant and the glazed bridges to the deck. On the De Boelelaan the VU hoofdgebouw (1973) stands as the slab towers with their storey ledges and window bands, the blue griffin and lettering on top, the lamp lattice, the low wings' window grid and the entrance hall under its canopy. Both measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: Loods 6, Atlanta, Gebouw Parnas and the Andaz: four more bespoke landmarks
notes.text: Round-4 lanes. Loods 6 on the KNSM-laan is the 190 m former KNSM warehouse in its pale render, with the rows of warehouse windows, the quay doors and the roof lights. Atlanta on the Stadhouderskade (1927) stands in red brick with its oriels, tower and the 1955 glass top storey. On the Zuidas, Gebouw Parnas is the 57 m Parnassustoren with its two slabs and the bridge building on A-frame trestles across the Parnassusweg. On the Prinsengracht the Andaz hotel is the 1974 public library again: four brick planes, three recessed glazed strips with glass roofs and the stone band above the ground floor. All measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: The Oostergasfabriek pool house and the Artis Planetarium
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks in Oost. The Sportfondsenbad Oost is the 1886 retort house of the Oostergasfabriek on the Land van Cocagneplein, with its twin gabled halls, round-headed iron windows and the tall chimney; the pool was fitted into it in 1929. Beside the Artis entrance on the Plantage Kerklaan the planetarium now has its dark standing-seam dome on a pale drum with sixteen piers, the glazed one-storey hall with its three prows and the two-storey entrance block. Both measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: Kraanspoor on its crane track, and Het Zonnehuis in Tuindorp Oostzaan
notes.text: Two Noord landmarks from the round-4 lanes. Kraanspoor at the NDSM: the 1952 concrete crane track on its arched legs over the harbour, the numbered stair cores and the three-storey glass office of 2007 set on top. On the Zonneplein the 1932 Zonnehuis is its real T-plan: the tall brick hall with the piers, canopy, granite steps and gilt lettering on the front, the four statue piers at the back, and both wings with their yellow fascia, measured from the city panoramas and open photographs. The box still reads as a blue glass grid where the real skin is pale translucent louvres; that material is on the list.

notes.title: The Barbizon Palace row and the Marinekazerne wall
notes.text: Two more bespoke landmarks from the round-3 lanes. The Barbizon Palace on the Prins Hendrikkade is now its real row: the hotel block with its roof lettering and the five old houses joined to it, with their neck gables, shop transoms and the French windows round the corner on the Zeedijk. On the Kattenburgerstraat the 1657 Marinekazerne wall runs its full length with the gate pediment, the blind niches cut into the brick, the dormers on the cornice and the corner front with its bricked-up doorway. Both measured from the city panoramas and open photographs.

notes.title: Far road paint settles into the road
notes.text: Lane lines, zebra crossings and the red of cycle paths now soften into the road surface in the distance, so the horizon reads calmer while the paint near you stays sharp.

notes.title: Seven more landmarks: Vijzelbank, the Carlton, Jan Wils' Citroën garage, Odeon, the Doelen, the W Hotel exchange and the Telegraaf
notes.text: Round three of the bespoke landmark lanes, all measured from the city panoramas and open photographs. The Vijzelbank (the former ABN AMRO block, now Prins en Keizer) with its stacked terraces, pale floor bands, white fins, colonnade and the Kerkstraat passage; the Carlton Hotel on the Vijzelstraat with its pointed-arch arcade, twelve bays of oriels on stone consoles, the bridge over the Reguliersdwarsstraat and the mansard. Jan Wils' white 1931 Citroën garage on the Stadionplein, ribbon windows, glazed stair tower and the lettering ring on the roof. Odeon on the Singel, Vingboons' 1662 front with its arched neck gable and claw pieces, and the Doelen Hotel on the Amstel corner (1883) in red brick and cream stone with its clock tower, dome, militiamen and striped awnings. The former telephone exchange on the Spuistraat (Crouwel 1927, now the W Hotel) with the gold W and the glass box on the roof, and Staal's Telegraaf building on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal with its six groups of white-framed windows, glass-block panels and tower. New kit parts came with them: terrace bands, a wrap band, arched neck-gable crowns and digits for the pixel lettering.

notes.title: The far city fades into haze
notes.text: Distant streets now lose colour and detail toward the horizon, so the corridor ahead stands out, while landmarks such as the Westerkerk stay crisp.

notes.title: Nine more landmarks: two Amstel bridges, two pools, Berlage, Duiker and the Vingboons houses
notes.text: Round two of the bespoke landmark lanes. The Blauwbrug and the Magere Brug are now real bridges, not kit arches: the Blauwbrug with its three openings, ship-prow piers and eight crowned lantern pylons, the Magere Brug with its white double bascule, balance beams and nine arches, and the bike rides over both at the game's own deck height. Zwembad Het Marnix (Mecanoo 2006) with its wave logo, and the Zuiderbad behind the Rijksmuseum (1911, built as a cycling school) with its nine bays and stepped gables. The Bungehuis on the Spuistraat in stone with its pinnacles; the four Cromhouthuizen neck gables on the Herengracht (Vingboons 1662) and the six joined houses of the Waldorf Astoria at Herengracht 542–556; De Burcht, Berlage's diamond workers' union with its tower and crenellated front; and Duiker's Eerste Openluchtschool, the glass-and-concrete school inside the Cliostraat block, with its gatehouse. Every one measured from the city panoramas and open photographs; the Vondelparkpaviljoen turned out to be in the game already.

notes.title: Seven kiosks: the herring stands, Dr Falafel, Mr Blou and the Dumplings hut
notes.text: The small food kiosks a rider passes are landmarks now, built from one kiosk kit (glass kiosk, wooden herring kiosk, trailer; hatches, awnings, lattice shutters, planted roofs, pixel lettering) with each one's own measurements and colours from the city panoramas: Dr Falafel by the Nassaukade bridge, Mr Blou I Love You on the Elandsgracht, the Dumplings kiosk on the Nassauplein, Frens Haringhandel on the Koningsplein in its navy and ochre lattice, Stubbe's Haring at the Haarlemmersluis, Haringhandel Jonk on the Spui and the poster kiosk on the Museumplein. Footprints come from BAG panden, the city's stall register or OpenStreetMap. Pat's Poffertjes, Ramon's coffee kiosk, the Beatrixpark kiosk and the floating Bloemenmarkt stalls are held with reasons until the photos or the kit allow them.

notes.title: Front doors sit in their reveals
notes.text: Most Amsterdam houses have their front door set back in a brick or plastered reveal, and the kit houses drew every door flush. The kit can now cut the door and its fanlight into the wall with jamb linings, a soffit and a threshold step, at a depth measured per house type from the panoramas (0.25 m on the 1897 Helmersbuurt rows, 0.45 m on the 1931 Transvaalbuurt rows, 0.6 m plastered portieken on the 1899 Duivelseiland rows). Five Helmersbuurt and Transvaalbuurt rows are recompiled with it; the Duivelseiland rows are held because a pale plastered vestibule reads as a blank slab at a grazing angle until the kit can darken the inside of a cavity. Before on the left, after on the right, desktop then phone.

notes.title: The city's own street furniture: containers, lamp posts, shelters
notes.text: The ride is furnished from the city's registers now. Thirteen thousand underground-container tops stand where the waste register puts them, with yellow lids for glass and blue for paper; a hundred and twenty thousand lamp posts come from the BGT, maroon canal lanterns in the centre and light-grey hooked poles elsewhere; eleven hundred tram and bus shelters and two hundred and forty advertising columns join them. Every model was measured from the city's own street panoramas (a container column is 1.25 m high on a 1.45 m plate, a canal lantern 4.1 m to its finial). They are drawn only near the rider and cost about four draws a frame. The What's New page has a new Street furniture category with its own gallery. Pairs: Noordermarkt containers, a Pijp street's lamp posts on a phone, the Nassaukade shelter; before on the left, after on the right.

notes.title: White roofs keep their texture

notes.title: Your second ride starts faster
notes.text: The first time you ride, the game builds the city's street network on your device. It now keeps that build, so when you come back the ride is ready a few seconds sooner after you press Start, on phones most of all. Nothing is sent anywhere; the copy lives in your browser and is rebuilt if the city data changes.

notes.title: Back gardens get garden rooms
notes.text: Inside the canal-ring courts and the Oud-Zuid and De Pijp blocks, the small outbuildings that were plain grey boxes now read as the garden rooms they usually are: a flat-roofed room in oiled larch slats or matte-black boards, with a glass front and door facing the house, an anthracite frame and a lid that overhangs the walls. Which sheds qualify is decided from open data only: a BAG build year from 2005 on, or a measured white-membrane or glass roof, and at least six square metres (the smaller boxes are bin and bike stores). That is 226 rooms in the centre so far; every other shed and every neighbour is byte-identical to before. You only see them at close zoom from the garden side, so the ride itself is unchanged. The first image is before, the second after, the third the glass front, the fourth the PDOK orthophoto of the same Herengracht/Keizersgracht court.

notes.title: The ride starts sooner after you read the briefing
notes.text: While the briefing is on screen the game now builds the city's streets and routing in the background, for the city and mode you have picked. If you read the briefing for a few seconds, the ride starts about twice as fast afterwards (on a phone, roughly three seconds instead of seven). Tapping Start the instant the briefing appears is unchanged for now; that case is next.

notes.title: Eleven new landmarks, from the Olympic Stadium to the Lensbomen
notes.text: Six modelling lanes added eleven buildings and one sculpture today, each built from the city panoramas, Commons photographs and the BAG outline: the Olympisch Stadion with its Marathontoren and flame bowl, Het Nieuwe Huis on the Roelof Hartplein with its clock tower, the Academie van Bouwkunst on Waterlooplein (the pedimented Huiszittenhuis and the stepped-gable Turfpakhuizen), the Hollandsche Manege gateway on the Vondelstraat, Amstelstation with its glazed hall and clock, Droogbak by the rail viaduct west of Central Station with its glazed courtyard roof, the Havengebouw slab on the IJ, the ABN AMRO head office on the Zuidas, De Wolkenkrabber at the head of the Amstelkanaal, Huis met de Hoofden on the Keizersgracht with its six sculpted heads, and the Lensbomen, Thom Puckey’s three bronze trees with six lenses on the old Binnengasthuis grounds. Every model passed the geometry audit, the facade comparison against the photographs and the inventory check; the Lensbomen also got a fun fact.

notes.title: Museumkwartier: the first measured rows inside the ring
notes.text: Two survey lanes photographed every block face of the five Museumkwartier buurten (Cornelis Schuyt, Concertgebouw, Hondecoeter, Johannes Vermeer and Duivelseiland, 2,000 pands) and found that none of the existing type libraries fits their 1890–1910 designs. Six new measured types were written and thirty pands stand in six rows: Van Breestraat 123–129 (gable-and-balcony row with step and bell gables), Cornelis Anthoniszstraat 62–70 and Balthasar Floriszstraat 2A–8 and 20–26 (the 1899 corbel-cornice rows), Wouwermanstraat 10–18 (glazed oriels) and Nicolaas Maesstraat 47–61 (lintel-and-parapet row). The kit grew a corbel table, stepped stone courses under oriels and a flat cap on neck and bell gables. The strip-over-model sheets show the photo above the model at the same scale.

notes.title: Amsterdam's buildings now load from compiled city cells
notes.text: The ride used to download the city's buildings as map tiles and work out their roofs, colours and neighbours on your device while you rode. The whole city is now compiled in advance into 9.7 MB of cells; a ride fetches only the cells around it, and the game's workers unpack them off the main thread. The buildings themselves do not change: at the five check spots the picture is pixel-identical to the old path. Expect fewer hitches as new streets stream in. If anything looks wrong, add ?world=live to the address to ride the old path and tell us.

notes.title: The bike leans into its turns, and only as much as the turn
notes.text: Since the lean arrived on 30 October a tap on a steering key rolled the bike to its full 19° at once, and onto the outside of the turn, so from the chase camera it looked like it had fallen over while riding straight. The lean now follows the turn the bike is actually making (speed times yaw rate, as a real bicycle does), stays at zero while the bike rides straight however the key is held, and rolls into the turn.

notes.text: On the new engine (?engine=own) the ride could begin with only a couple of blocks drawn and the rest arriving over the next seconds, because behind the loading screen the buildings were styled far too slowly. notes.title: No colour step at the edge of the detailed city
notes.text: The simplified ground beyond the detailed area now uses the same asphalt, klinker and pavement colours as the streets around you, so the roads no longer change colour in the distance, as they did by the RAI.

notes.title: Surprise rides no longer finish next to the start
notes.text: A surprise ride could draw a finish 45 metres from its start (Micropia and Artis share a street), fail with "Start and finish are too close" and drop you back at setup. The picker now draws again among places at least 200 metres away; rides that already worked start exactly as before.

notes.title: Fewer hitches as new facades arrive
notes.text: The work that prepares a block of facades for drawing (sorting its footprints into tiles, finding each house's neighbours, matching streets) does the same job in a third to a half of the time, with identical results. On a slow machine the longest hitch while riding through the Jordaan dropped from a tenth of a second to about half that.

Two kit fixes made this possible: a saddle roof under a pointed gable no longer overlaps the gable's brick, and a row's crown comes from its type unless the panorama's skyline is really sky (branches over the roofline used to become gables). Ten pands; the rest of the family is held until the kit can draw shared gables, white dormers and the low shouldered gables these streets favour.

notes.title: Clicking an ordinary building no longer freezes the ride
notes.text: Since building facts started loading on the first click (31 October), a click on a house with a register year but no article asked for its facts again from inside its own refresh, forever, and the page stopped responding. One request per card now; the year card opens and the rest fills in once.

notes.title: Amsterdam's streets load three times faster
notes.text: The Amsterdam street network now arrives as a compact binary file instead of a 14 MB JSON document: the same streets, decoded bit for bit (a test pins the published file to the shipped data), fetched and parsed in about 60 ms where it took 200. Routes, turn names and the reachability of every named spot are byte-identical. Other cities keep their JSON until their binaries are published.

notes.title: Long routes no longer freeze as canals and bridges load
notes.text: Preparing a new ground cell used to stall the ride for up to half a second on long routes while it tested every canal polygon and every street segment for openings under footbridges. Those tests now skip polygons and segments that cannot contain the point (same result, byte-identical across the city). On the seeded Anne Frank → Rijksmuseum ride the long tasks went from 10 to 0 and the longest frame from 600 to 68 ms; a city-wide preparation run fell from 25 to 6 s.

notes.title: Fewer hitches when new ground streams in
notes.text: Riding into a new part of the city, the game no longer freezes for a moment while the next ground cell is prepared: the preparation now yields between its steps, the road index behind bridge decks only covers the roads it needs, and landmarks re-seat on the ground in small slices. On a 60 s Jordaan ride the frames over 50 ms went from 7 to 0 and the longest frame from 92 to 40 ms.

notes.title: Roads run across the Kinkerbrug and the Beltbrug
notes.text: Thirty-nine road bridges whose decks were missing from the bridge register, among them the Kinkerbrug on the Postjesweg, the Beltbrug on the Jan van Galenstraat, De Clercqstraat and Nassauplein, now carry their asphalt and tram rails across the water instead of a pale paved slab.

notes.title: Rail bridges on piers, open platforms at Amstel
notes.text: Railway bridges stand on piers with steel girders over the water, Centraal's tracks and platforms sit at platform height under the shed, and Amsterdam Amstel's platforms have separate canopies instead of one flat white slab, without the brick houses that stood under the tracks.

notes.title: One tap of a turn button sets you off
notes.text: On a phone, where the bike stops and waits for a side (a T-junction, or a ride that starts across a street), a single tap of the left or right button now takes that turn straight away. Before, a tap only queued the turn and the bike stood still until the button was held. A very quick tap is no longer lost between two frames either. Holding still works, and straight streets ride as before.

notes.title: Steering that feels the same on every screen
notes.text: The bike now drives the same on a 30 Hz laptop, a 60 Hz desktop and a 120 Hz phone: the physics steps in fixed 1/120 s substeps, so a corner taken at the same speed lands in the same place everywhere (within 5 cm; before, 30 Hz could be off by 2.6 m). The camera follows the rider in the rider's own frame, so it no longer trails behind at speed or surges when a frame runs long, looks 16 px ahead along the street and pulls back 10 % as you speed up. notes.text: Lanes, car parks and loading bays that buildings were drawn standing on are open now: Staalmeesterslaan, Gerard Ruttenhof, the VUmc, Stadionplein, Cruquiusweg, the Ankerweg warehouse and the Oosterdoksstraat, with the building carried over the road where it really bridges it. notes.text: The approaches to the IJ, Piet Hein, Spaarndammer and Michiel de Ruijter tunnels are walled cuts now, sinking to a dark tunnel mouth, so the IJ-tunnel ramp by NEMO no longer looks like a street you could ride up (bikes stay out of motor tunnels). Cycle and foot underpasses under rail embankments and dikes, like the Molukkenstraat and the Cuyperspassage, ride under the embankment instead of climbing over it.

notes.title: Ride through the poorts
notes.text: Streets, cycle paths and alleys that run under a building are open now, with the building carried over them: the poorts into Jordaan hofjes, the Motorwal, and the path under the Jan van Zutphenstraat towers. Buildings OSM left without a height are measured from the AHN height map instead of all standing at 9 m, so those towers rise to 37 m and garden sheds sit low.

notes.title: Buildings out of the road
notes.text: Underground metro halls and car parks no longer stand across the Weesperstraat, Wibautstraat or the Albert Cuyp, and the Holocaust Namenmonument faces the right way. Amstel station stands again, with its bus canopy raised over the platforms. Canopies are thin roofs instead of solid blocks, and houses built over a street, as on the Kerkstraat, start at the right storey.

notes.title: Ride off from a standstill on squares
notes.text: A bike that stopped on an open square such as the Nieuwmarkt could only back up; squares now ride like paving, so it pulls away forward again.
